excerpt: Blender's GPU Accelerated UI, Decoupled from it's original codebase. Supports Rust, Python, JS, React, C & C++. Twice as good as GPUI - ppmpreetham/BUI
content_html:
Blender's user interface, as a library you can use from Python, Rust, JavaScript (React, Svelte), C, C++ and Dear ImGui.

People spent decades building and optimizing Blender's GUI. It's battery and memory efficient, and super duper fast. We decoupled it, to give everyone a chance to build their own products with it. It supports multiple languages and frameworks, so you won't miss a beat!

Website and full documentation: bui.preetham.top · Chat: Discord

This README is a small book. Read it front to back for the whole story, or jump to the chapter you need. Every chapter links to a longer guide in docs/ or on the website when there's more to say.

Part I: Welcome

1. What BUI is

BUI takes the user interface of Blender (its widget drawing, its interaction rules and its look) and turns it into a standalone UI library with a small C core. Your code builds the widget tree and handles callbacks. Layout, input, drawing and presenting all happen in fast native code, on the CPU or the GPU.

At the heart of BUI is the kit: a small runtime written in C. The kit holds every widget in one tree, lays them out, handles the mouse and keyboard, and draws them the way Blender does. The drawing code is a C port of Blender's own widget code, and the interaction follows Blender's rules. On top of the kit sit bindings: thin layers that let Python, Rust, JavaScript, C++ and Dear ImGui talk to it.

What BUI is not:

  • Not Blender. It contains the parts of Blender's UI code it needs and builds on its own. You don't need Blender installed, and you don't need to know Blender to use it.
  • Not a browser. The Rust and JavaScript sides use HTML and CSS as a UI language, but there's no browser engine, no webview and no network.
  • Not a re-imagining. The widget drawing is ported from Blender's interface_widgets.cc, and the Dear ImGui support runs the real Dear ImGui.

2. Why BUI exists

Blender's interface is famous for how it feels. You press a number field and drag: the cursor vanishes, the value glides under your hand, and you never hit the edge of the screen. You type 2*pi into a field and it just works. You type "ad cu" into a menu and it finds "Add Cube". Millions of artists have these habits in their hands.

That interface is also fast and frugal. It redraws only what changed, sleeps when nothing does, and starts in milliseconds. BUI exists so that any app, in any language, can have both: Blender's feel, and Blender's efficiency.

3. Who it's for

  • You have a tkinter app and wish it looked less like 1998. Run it on BUI, unchanged.
  • You're building a tool for artists who already know Blender. Give them the panels, sliders and shortcuts their hands expect.
  • You write Rust or React and want a native desktop UI without shipping a browser.
  • You use Dear ImGui and want it to look and feel like Blender, with one build flag.
  • You're curious how a UI toolkit works. The source is readable, and the concepts are explained in plain words.

Before you ship something with BUI, read the known limitations: no accessibility support yet, no input methods, and it looks like Blender, not like your operating system.

4. Pick your language

You can drive BUI many ways, and all of them share the same C runtime, so they all get the same widgets and interactions:

You write You get Status
tkinter code, even existing programs, unchanged Blender-styled apps; every tkinter and ttk API Complete
Qt-style Python (QWidget, layouts, clicked.connect) The common subset of Qt widgets Partial
Blender components (Panel, NumberSlider, PieMenu, the node editor ...) 45 native Blender widgets and editors, from Python; ten of them also from Rust and JavaScript Complete
Rust: HTML + CSS + Tailwind, HTML-like markup (rsx! / view!), hooks, or gpui / zopra syntax A web-like framework: HTML that looks like a browser's, Blender's look with styled, and Blender components (<NumberSlider>, <Button> ...) Working
JavaScript / React / Svelte on Node.js or Bun: a DOM-like API, JSX or Svelte components The same engine and components in native windows, over napi-rs; React's hooks backed by signals; Svelte 5 components Working
Dear ImGui from C++, C, Python or Rust The real Dear ImGui on BUI windows in Blender's theme, or a build where ImGui's widgets are Blender's widgets Working
C (BUI_kit.h) The kit itself: nodes, widgets, windows Working
MyGo MyGo Not yet (coming soon)

Not sure which to pick? If you already have code, use the row that matches it. If you're starting fresh in Python, the Blender components are the friendliest.

5. Features at a glance

Blender's widgets and interactions

  • Number fields you drag with a hidden, continuous cursor: Shift for precision, Ctrl to snap.
  • Math in number fields, with Blender's own expression evaluator: 2*pi, min(4, 3), round(1.7), x if c else y.
  • Ctrl+Wheel steps values, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy values, Backspace resets.
  • Drag across checkboxes to set them all.
  • Press-drag-release menus, pie menus, and Blender's fuzzy menu search: "ad cu" finds "Add Cube", typos are forgiven, recent picks rank first.
  • Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z on every UI edit, and inside a text field while you type; Tab between fields.
  • Blender's float display precision, multi-field vertical drags, and panels that collapse with Blender's animation.
  • The HSV color wheel, color ramps, curves, trees, lists, text areas, canvases, a node editor and Blender's File Browser.
  • Blender's Dark and Light themes, switchable at run time.

Python

  • tkinter: all 7,846 public names of tkinter and ttk. Nine real programs behave identically on the standard library and on BUI.
  • Qt syntax: widgets, layouts, signals, QPainter, menus and timers.
  • Components: 45 Blender widgets, editors and templates.
  • Dear ImGui: from blenderui import imgui, pyimgui-style.
  • One pip install, no Qt or Tk widgets drawing anything.

Rust: HTML and CSS, without a browser

  • All 113 HTML elements, drawn like a browser draws them; styled gives any subtree Blender's look, and Blender components (<NumberSlider>, <Button>, <ColorSwatch> ...) are real Blender widgets.
  • Modern CSS: flexbox, grid with named areas, tables, calc() and every math function, var(), oklch() and color-mix(), :has(), nesting, @layer, @media ranges, @container, ::before/::after, counters.
  • Effects and motion: @keyframes animations and transitions, filters, backdrop-filter, blend modes, clip-path, masks, 2D transforms, border-image.
  • Tailwind CSS v4: class="md:hover:bg-sky-500/50" or bare attributes (<div p-4 bg-[#4772b3]>), with "did you mean" compile errors.
  • rsx! / view! HTML-like markup, #[component], and hooks in zopra, React or Leptos style (use_state, signal, Memo, Effect, context).
  • gpui-compatible syntax too: div().flex().gap_2(), Render, cx.listener.
  • On crates.io: cargo add blenderui.

Fast by design

  • Damage rendering: an idle UI costs 0% CPU, and a hover redraws only the widget it touches.
  • Opt-in GPU renderer (Direct3D 11 on Windows, OpenGL 3.3 on Linux), modeled on Blender's instanced widget drawing. It draws the same pixels as the CPU raster.
  • In the benchmark, 2–4× less CPU per frame than gpui-fast, with less RAM and a ~5 ms first frame.
  • Blender's text: Inter (Blender's UI font) is embedded and rendered with FreeType the way Blender renders it, so text looks the same on every platform. On the GPU, glyphs are drawn from their outlines with Slug, falling back to a per-glyph atlas like Blender's.

Images

  • One decoder set for every language, in C: PNG, GIF, BMP, TGA, QOI (Wuffs, memory-safe), JPEG (libjpeg-turbo), WebP including animated (libwebp), Radiance HDR, PNM and SVG. The design is Blender's imbuf: one image type and a format table.
  • Decoded at the size it is drawn, off the UI thread: JPEG thumbnails use DCT scaling (a 4K photo becomes a 256 px thumbnail in ~12 ms), visible images first, scrolled-away requests cancelled, and only the image's rectangle redraws when it arrives. The page never jumps: sizes come from the file header.
  • One memory-budgeted cache (256 MiB by default). Scrolling 1,000 photo thumbnails: 2.9 ms p99 frames and 100 MB, against 96 ms and 2.5 GB when decoding on the UI thread; 0 allocations in a settled frame, every block freed at exit. Images.
  • Animated GIF and WebP play everywhere an image shows, decoded one frame at a time at the size drawn (two frames held per animation), each frame for its own delay, only the image's rectangle repainting. Off screen, scrolled away or in a hidden window they pause: 200 animations at once take 0.76 ms p50 / 1.5 ms p99 render frames, and nothing at all once off screen. frame holds one frame; reduced motion holds them all.
  • Large images on the GPU: images over 2047 px get a texture of their own on Direct3D 11 and OpenGL (tiled only past the device limit), freed with the image.
  • Video: <video> in every language, decoded by the OS (Media Foundation with DXVA, GStreamer, AVFoundation; loaded at run time) at the size drawn, frames in one GPU texture per player updated in place, YCbCr converted in the shader, and nothing decoded off screen. 1080p plays at 0.99 ms render frames and 9 % of a core on the GPU renderer, five at once at 28 %, with 0 allocations per frame. Play, pause, seek, rate, loop, poster, state events, and Blender-style controls. Video.
  • <img>, CSS background-image, object-fit, Blender Image components, tkinter PhotoImage (now also JPEG, WebP, BMP, TGA, QOI, HDR, SVG), canvas items, data-table image columns, chat-list media and Dear ImGui textures (animated ones too).

JavaScript and React

  • React 19.3 renders to BUI: HTML host components, CSS and Tailwind, events, Suspense, transitions, actions, and Blender components (<NumberSlider>, <Button> ...). BUI draws them, on the CPU or the GPU; there's no browser and no webview.
  • React's hooks, by React's names, holding signals: pass one into JSX ({count}) and a change updates that one node without re-rendering; read it while rendering (count.value) and the component re-renders, as with React. A conformance suite checks each hook against React's own.
  • Svelte 5 (@blender-ui/svelte): components with runes, snippets, bindings and scoped styles, mounted into native windows; Svelte's compiled code runs on BUI's DOM, so a $state change updates the one node that shows it.
  • @blender-ui/native: a DOM-like API (createElement, appendChild, addEventListener) with the same signals, for apps without a framework, and the shared layer the React and Svelte bindings are thin adapters over.
  • Node.js and Bun, through a napi-rs addon, with headless mode for tests.

Small standalone apps

  • bui build app.jsx produces one executable of 6.3 to 6.9 MB (by the features it uses): BUI with an embedded QuickJS engine.
  • First frame in ~70 ms, at 19 MB of RAM, with nothing to install. There's no browser and no webview.
  • --bun builds a Bun executable instead, with Node's APIs and a JIT.
  • Builds take under a second: the app's bundle is appended to a prebuilt runtime.
  • Pay for what you use: one feature table (features.json) drives CMake options, cargo features and bui build, which links the smallest runtime an app needs: 6.3 MB for hello world, 6.9 MB with images or video. Binary size.

Dear ImGui

  • The real Dear ImGui 1.93: every function of imgui.h works, including ShowDemoWindow().
  • Four languages: C++ (drop-in imgui.h), C (cimgui.h, all 399 functions), Python and Rust (generated from imgui.h).
  • Blender's look: Blender's theme colors and metrics with Inter; or, with BUI_IMGUI_BLENDER_WIDGETS=ON, Blender's actual widgets and interaction, pixel-identical to BUI's own.
  • Idle costs nothing: frames run only on input and while something animates.

Native everywhere

  • Native windows on Windows (Win32) and Linux (X11, Wayland through XWayland), and an experimental Cocoa host for macOS ported from Blender's GHOST.
  • HiDPI: per-monitor DPI on Windows, Xft.dpi on Linux, Retina on macOS.
  • Headless mode for tests and screenshots, with a virtual clock that steps animations exactly.
  • On Linux, libX11 and libGL are loaded at run time, so BUI imports on servers without them.

Part II: Getting started

7. Install

Python. You need CPython 3.11 or newer. Wheels are published for Windows, Linux and macOS, so there's nothing to compile. One package gives you all four Python APIs (tkinter syntax, Qt syntax, the Blender components and Dear ImGui):

pip install blenderui
python -c "import blenderui; print(blenderui.__version__)"

Import it as blenderui. You'll also see import bui in older examples: it's the same code under its original name, but an unrelated project owns bui on PyPI, so prefer blenderui in anything you publish.

Rust. The crate is blenderui on crates.io:

cargo add blenderui

The first build compiles BUI's C kit for you, so you need Rust 1.88 or newer, CMake and a C compiler (on Windows, the Visual Studio Build Tools for the default MSVC target), and on Linux the X11 headers (libx11-dev or libX11-devel; no GL headers are needed).

JavaScript. You need Node.js 18 or newer, or Bun:

npm install @blender-ui/react react     # or: bun add @blender-ui/react react
npm install @blender-ui/svelte svelte   # Svelte 5
npm install @blender-ui/native          # the DOM-like API, without React

The npm packages are prebuilt for Windows x64. On Linux, build the addon from a clone (npm install then npm run build in bindings/, with Rust, CMake and a C compiler); windows are native X11 windows there. On macOS, JavaScript runs headless for now (see Platforms).

C and C++. Build from source with CMake 3.20+ and a C11 / C++20 compiler (MSVC, GCC or MinGW-w64, or Clang); on Linux, also the X11 headers:

git clone https://github.com/ppmpreetham/BUI && cd BUI
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build -j 2
ctest --test-dir build            # optional: run the test suites

In your own CMake project, add BUI as a subdirectory and link bui::kit (or bui::imgui for Dear ImGui):

add_subdirectory(BUI)
target_link_libraries(myapp PRIVATE bui::kit)

Dear ImGui. Python gets it with pip install blenderui (import blenderui.imgui). C++ links bui::imgui, C links bui_cimgui. Rust uses the blenderui-imgui crate:

cargo add blenderui-imgui

If something goes wrong:

Symptom Fix
ImportError: buipy You're running from a source checkout without a build. Build first (cmake --build build), or set BUIPY_BUILD_DIR. The extension must match your Python version.
The window never appears Start the event loop: mainloop(), app.exec() or App.run().
Blurry or tiny UI Set BUI_UI_SCALE, for example BUI_UI_SCALE=1.25.
gpu=True does nothing Run with BUI_GPU_DEBUG=1 to see why the GPU device didn't start. Without Direct3D 11 or OpenGL 3.3, BUI stays on the CPU renderer, which draws the same pixels.

More: docs/getting-started.md and Install BUI on the website.

8. First app: tkinter

Run any tkinter program on BUI without changing a line:

blenderui-tk my_app.py          # same as: python -m bui.tksyntax my_app.py

blenderui-tk makes import tkinter return BUI's implementation for that run. Or opt in from code:

import blenderui.tksyntax as tk
from blenderui.tksyntax import ttk, messagebox

root = tk.Tk()
name = tk.StringVar(value="Cube")
ttk.Entry(root, textvariable=name).pack(fill="x", padx=8, pady=8)
ttk.Button(root, text="Greet",
           command=lambda: messagebox.showinfo("Hi", "Hello " + name.get())).pack()
root.mainloop()

That snippet is only a window with an entry and a button. These two are larger, unchanged programs from examples/site/, running on BUI:


Unchanged tkinter and ttk programs (examples/site/tk_export.py, ttk_queue.py)

Number fields (Spinbox, Scale) scrub like Blender's, Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z undo edits, and filedialog opens Blender's File Browser. Guide: docs/tkinter.md.

9. First app: Blender components

Build with Blender's own components:

from blenderui.components import App, Panel, NumberSlider, VectorField, Checkbox, ColorSwatch, Button

App("Object", (420, 520),
    Panel("Transform",
          VectorField("Location", (0.0, 1.25, 0.0)),
          NumberSlider("Scale", 1.0, min=0, max=10, on_change=print)),
    Panel("Shading",
          Checkbox("Shadows", True),
          ColorSwatch("Color", (0.8, 0.3, 0.1, 1.0))),
    Button("Apply", on_click=lambda: print("apply")),
).run()

That snippet is a small window. This is a bigger program built from the same components, a Render Properties editor:


A Render Properties editor from the components (examples/site/render_props.py)

There are 45 components: layout, values, buttons, views, menus and pie menus, the color picker, the color ramp, curve and node editors, areas and templates. Reference: docs/components.md.

10. First app: Qt syntax

Write Qt-style Python. The import is the only line that differs from PySide or PyQt, and neither is needed:

import sys
from blenderui.qtsyntax import (QApplication, QWidget, QVBoxLayout, QFormLayout,
                                QLineEdit, QComboBox, QSlider, QProgressBar,
                                QPushButton, QLabel, Qt)

app = QApplication(sys.argv)
window = QWidget()
window.setWindowTitle("Export")
layout = QVBoxLayout(window)

form = QFormLayout()
kind = QComboBox()
kind.addItems(["glTF", "FBX", "OBJ"])
quality = QSlider(Qt.Horizontal)
quality.setRange(0, 100)
form.addRow("Format:", kind)
form.addRow("Quality:", quality)
layout.addLayout(form)

bar = QProgressBar()
quality.valueChanged.connect(bar.setValue)
layout.addWidget(bar)

status = QLabel("Ready.")
go = QPushButton("Export")
go.clicked.connect(lambda: status.setText("Exporting as " + kind.currentText()))
layout.addWidget(status)
layout.addWidget(go)

window.show()
sys.exit(app.exec())

A bigger program in the same syntax, a material editor (not the output of the snippet above):


Qt syntax (examples/site/qt_material.py)

Qt syntax is partial (about 24% of Qt's method names on the main widget classes); anything missing raises AttributeError. Guide: docs/qt.md.

11. First app: Rust, in rsx and gpui builders

BUI's Rust crate has two first-class syntaxes, and they draw the same window:

  • rsx! is HTML-like markup inside a macro, with #[component] functions and hooks for state.
  • gpui builders are plain method chains: div().flex().gap_3().child(...). State lives in your view struct, and cx.listener updates it. gpui code compiles against BUI too.

In rsx! (this is bindings/rust/blenderui/examples/hello.rs; run it with cargo run --release --example hello in bindings/rust):

use blenderui::prelude::*;

#[component]
fn counter(label: &str) {
    let (count, set_count) = use_state(0);
    rsx! {
        <div flex items-center gap-3 p-4 rounded-xl bg-zinc-800>
            <span text-zinc-300>{label.to_string()} ": " {count().to_string()}</span>
            <div px-3 py-1 rounded-md bg-sky-700 hover:bg-sky-500 onClick={move || set_count(count() + 1)}>
                "Add one"
            </div>
        </div>
    }
}

struct Hello;

impl Render for Hello {
    fn render(&mut self, _: &mut Window, _: &mut Context<Self>) -> impl IntoElement {
        rsx! {
            <body m-0 p-6 min-h-screen flex flex-col gap-4 bg-zinc-900 text-white>
                <h1 text-2xl font-bold>"Hello, BUI"</h1>
                <counter label="Clicks" />
                <NumberSlider min={0.0} max={10.0} value="5" />   // a real Blender slider
            </body>
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    Application::new().run(|cx| {
        cx.open_window(WindowOptions::default(), |_, cx| cx.new(|_| Hello)).unwrap();
    });
}

In gpui builders, the same window:

use blenderui::prelude::*;

struct Hello { count: i32 }

impl Render for Hello {
    fn render(&mut self, _: &mut Window, cx: &mut Context<Self>) -> impl IntoElement {
        let counter = div().flex().items_center().gap_3().p_4().rounded_xl().bg(rgb(0x27272a))
            .child(span().text_color(rgb(0xd4d4d8)).child(format!("Clicks: {}", self.count)))
            .child(div().px_3().py_1().rounded_md().bg(rgb(0x0369a1))
                .hover(|s| s.bg(rgb(0x0ea5e9))).cursor_pointer()
                .child("Add one")
                .on_click(cx.listener(|this, _, _, cx| {
                    this.count += 1;
                    cx.notify();
                })));
        body().m_0().p_6().css("min-height", "100vh").flex().flex_col().gap_4()
            .bg(rgb(0x18181b)).text_color(white())
            .child(h1().text_2xl().font_bold().child("Hello, BUI"))
            .child(counter)
            .child(NumberSlider().min(0.0).max(10.0).value("5"))   // a real Blender slider
    }
}

fn main() {
    Application::new().run(|cx| {
        cx.open_window(WindowOptions::default(), |_, cx| cx.new(|_| Hello { count: 0 })).unwrap();
    });
}

Two small things that trip people up in rsx!:

  • Text children are text (&'static str, String, SharedString) or elements. Numbers and borrowed &str props aren't, so write {count().to_string()} and {label.to_string()}.
  • A component's body is a normal block that ends in markup, usually an rsx!.

Here's a bigger example, a render-farm dashboard, written once in each syntax. The two programs draw identical pixels:


site_dashboard.rs (rsx!) and site_dashboard_builder.rs (gpui builders)

Guide: docs/rust.md, and the Rust tutorial on the website.

12. First app: JavaScript and React

/** @jsxImportSource @blender-ui/react */
import { render, useState, NumberSlider } from "@blender-ui/react"

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0) // React's hook, holding a signal
  return (
    <main styled className="p-6 flex flex-col gap-3">
      {" "}
      {/* `styled`: Blender's look */}
      <span>Clicks: {count}</span>
      <button onClick={() => setCount((c) => c + 1)}>Add one</button>
      <NumberSlider min={0} max={10} /> {/* a Blender component */}
    </main>
  )
}

render(<Counter />, { title: "Counter", width: 360, height: 200, gpu: true })
bun app.jsx                    # run it (Bun reads JSX directly)
npx bui build app.jsx          # or ship it: app.exe, one 7 MB file

Without React, @blender-ui/native gives you a DOM-like API:

const { App, signal } = require("@blender-ui/native")

const app = new App({ gpu: true })
const win = app.window({ title: "Hello", width: 360, height: 200 })
win.body.className = "m-0 p-6 flex flex-col gap-3 bg-[#2b2b2b] text-[#e6e6e6]"

const clicks = signal(0)
const label = win.createElement("span")
label.textContent = clicks // follows the signal
const button = win.createElement("button")
button.textContent = "Add one"
button.addEventListener("click", () => clicks.value++)
win.body.appendChild(label)
win.body.appendChild(button)

These snippets are small. This is a larger example, a task list in React, and not the output of the code above:


A task list in React (examples/site/js/todo_react.js); the DOM-like version draws the same

Node.js 18+ or Bun. Prebuilt for Windows x64; on Linux, build the addon from source (npm run build in bindings/node) and windows are native. Guide: docs/javascript.md.

13. First app: Dear ImGui

The real Dear ImGui 1.93 runs on BUI: BUI's windows, input, CPU/GPU renderer, Blender's theme and the Inter font. Existing ImGui code compiles unchanged.

C++:

#include "imgui.h"
#include "imgui_impl_bui.h"     // see examples/imgui_demo.cpp

static void frame(void*) {
    ImGui::ShowDemoWindow();
    ImGui::Begin("Hello");
    static float v = 0.5f;
    ImGui::SliderFloat("Value", &v, 0.0f, 1.0f);
    ImGui::End();
}

int main() {
    ImGui::CreateContext();
    ImGui_ImplBUI_App* app = ImGui_ImplBUI_CreateApp("Demo", 1280, 800, frame, nullptr);
    ImGui_ImplBUI_RunApp(app);
    ImGui_ImplBUI_DestroyApp(app);
    ImGui::DestroyContext();
}

Python:

import blenderui.imgui as imgui        # C: cimgui.h  ·  Rust: the blenderui-imgui crate

state = {"value": 0.5}

def frame():
    imgui.show_demo_window()
    imgui.begin("Hello")
    _, state["value"] = imgui.slider_float("Value", state["value"], 0.0, 1.0)
    imgui.end()

imgui.run(frame, title="Hello", size=(1280, 800))

C (cimgui.h, cimgui conventions: ImGui_Button, ImGui_ButtonEx, and the backend in cimgui_impl_bui.h) and Rust (blenderui-imgui) work the same way:

use blenderui_imgui as imgui;

14. First app: C

The kit's API is one header, kit/include/BUI_kit.h, and it doubles as the reference: every function has a one-line comment. This is a shortened examples/kit_hello.c: a slider and a button in a native window.

#include <stdio.h>
#include "BUI_kit.h"

static void on_event(void *data, BKNode *node, int kind, void *ref, double a, double b)
{
  if (kind == BK_EV_CLICK) printf("clicked %s\n", BK_get_str(node, "text"));
  else if (kind == BK_EV_CHANGE) printf("%s = %g\n", BK_get_str(node, "label"), BK_get_num(node, "value"));
}

int main(void)
{
  BKNode *root = BK_node_new("frame");          /* everything is a node */
  BK_set_num(root, "padding", 8);               /* configured by property name */

  BKNode *size = BK_node_new("slider");
  BK_set_str(size, "label", "Size");
  BK_set_num(size, "max", 10);
  BK_set_num(size, "value", 2.5);
  BK_node_add(root, size, -1);
  BK_geom_set_manager(size, BK_GEOM_PACK);      /* Tk's packer, in C */
  BK_geom_set(size, "fill", 1);

  BKNode *apply = BK_node_new("button");
  BK_set_str(apply, "text", "Apply");
  BK_node_add(root, apply, -1);
  BK_geom_set_manager(apply, BK_GEOM_PACK);

  BKContext *ctx = BK_context_new(root);        /* input, focus, popups, undo */
  BKHost host = {0};
  host.emit = on_event;                         /* the window fills in the rest */
  BK_context_set_host(ctx, &host);

  if (BK_window_supported()) {                  /* Win32, X11 or Cocoa */
    BKWindow *win = BK_window_new(ctx, "BUI from C", 320, 120);
    BK_window_show(win);
    BK_window_run();
    BK_window_free(win);
  }
  BK_context_free(ctx);
  BK_node_free(root);
  return 0;
}

Part III: Concepts

15. How it works

 your code:   tkinter   Qt   components   Dear ImGui (C++/C/Python/Rust)   Rust: rsx! / HTML / CSS / Tailwind / hooks   JS / React
                  │      │        │                │                                  │                                    │
                  └──── Python: options, signals    │ ImGui core + BUI backend          └── style cascade + taffy layout ◄────┘
                                  │                │                                  │
 C kit (kit/):   node tree · geometry · input & interaction · Blender widget drawing · undo · animation · themes · Blender search/expr
                                         │
 renderer:       damage-driven software raster (parallel)   or   GPU (Direct3D 11 / OpenGL 3.3, instanced, opt-in)
                                         │
 window:         native Win32 / X11 / Cocoa window   ·   stdlib Tk window   ·   headless (tests, screenshots)
  1. Your code, in any language above, creates widgets and says what happens when they change.
  2. The kit keeps them in one tree, lays them out and handles input, following Blender's rules.
  3. The renderer draws them, on the CPU by default or on the GPU if you ask.
  4. Damage rendering keeps it cheap: a change redraws only the rectangle it touched, and an idle window uses no CPU at all.

What's under the hood:

  • Blender's real UI code. Widget drawing is a C port of Blender's interface_widgets.cc (round_box_edges, widgetbase_draw, the shape tables), and interaction follows interface_handlers.cc. Color math, rects, text cursors, string search and expression evaluation are Blender's blenlib, copied in. A few interface files (string search, text-edit undo, float precision) are copied into kit/intern/blender/ and edited for the kit. The X11 and Cocoa hosts follow Blender's GHOST; the Win32 host is BUI's own.
  • One node tree. Every widget is one kit node. The C kit owns layout, hit testing, hover, focus, drags, menus, tooltips, undo and animation.
  • Damage rendering. A change marks only its widget's rectangle, and only changed tiles reach the screen.
  • Thin bindings. Python, Rust and JavaScript keep only what their syntax layer needs.

More: ARCHITECTURE.md and How it works.

16. Blender's widgets and interactions

These rules live in the C kit, so they work the same everywhere Blender widgets are drawn: the Python components, tkinter and Qt syntax, the Rust and JavaScript Blender components and form controls inside styled, ImGui's Blender-widgets build, and every C kit widget.

  • Drag to scrub. Press a number field and drag sideways. The cursor hides and wraps, so you never hit the screen edge, and comes back where the drag started. A float moves one click step per pixel; Shift moves at a tenth of the speed; Esc cancels and restores the value.
  • Ctrl snaps with Blender's rules: unbounded floats to whole units, angles to 10°, sliders to 0.1, 1 or 10 depending on their range, integers to multiples of 10.
  • Click to type, and type math: Blender's expression evaluator (expr_pylike_eval.cc) turns 2*pi, 90/4, min(4, 3) or x if c else y into numbers. This works in Blender number fields and sliders; plain text fields keep what you type as text.
  • Shortcuts on any value: Backspace resets to the default, - negates, Ctrl+Wheel steps, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy and paste, right-click opens Copy, Paste and Reset.
  • Several fields at once. Drag down over a column of number fields to collect them, then sideways to change them together. Drag across checkboxes (or panel headers) to set them all in one stroke.
  • Panels collapse with Blender's animation; Ctrl+click opens one and closes the others; drag the grip to reorder.
  • Menus work press-drag-release or click; hover switches menu-bar menus; pie menus open around the pointer.
  • Menu search is Blender's string search: start typing in any open menu. It matches word initials ("ad cu" finds "Add Cube"), forgives typos, and ranks your recent picks first.
  • Undo everywhere. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z work on every UI edit, and inside a text field while you type. A burst of typing or a multi-field drag is one step.
  • Float precision follows Blender: small values show the decimals they need.
  • Tooltips appear after Blender's half-second delay.

Coming soon: typing values with units ("2 m"), Blender's search-as-you-type popups, and widget drag and drop. More: Blender's widgets.

18. Rendering on the CPU and the GPU

BUI has two renderers, and they draw the same pixels.

  • The software raster (gpu/intern/gpu_raster.c) is the default. It draws anti-aliased shapes with signed-distance coverage, like Blender's widget shaders, into one frame buffer, compares it with the last frame in 64×32 tiles, and reports only the tiles that changed. Big canvases draw in parallel bands on Windows (BUI_RASTER_THREADS). It needs nothing from your graphics card and uses the least memory.
  • The GPU renderer is opt-in: Direct3D 11 on Windows (gpu/intern/gpu_d3d11.c) and OpenGL 3.3 core on Linux (gpu/intern/gpu_gl.c). It's modeled on Blender's instanced widget drawing: each primitive is one 128-byte instance of a single uber-shader, so a frame is a few instanced draw calls. Text and images are cached in atlases. Frames render into a persistent target, so only damaged regions redraw; on Windows, a flip-model swap chain presents dirty rectangles. On Linux, libGL, libEGL and libX11 are loaded at run time (GLX for windows, EGL for offscreen), so no GL headers are needed, and BUI falls back to the CPU where OpenGL is missing.

The shaders evaluate the software raster's formulas: the parity test finds 10 of 172,800 pixels that differ by more than 3/255, on both backends.

Turn the GPU on:

Where How
Python bui.set_gpu(True) before creating windows; tkinter syntax also tk.Tk(gpu=True)
Rust Application::new().gpu(true), or WindowOptions { gpu: Some(true), .. }
JavaScript new App({ gpu: true }), or React's render(..., { gpu: true })
C BUI_gpu_set_default(1), or BK_window_set_gpu(win, 1)
Any app, no code change BUI_GPU=1

BUI_GPU=1 overrides the app-wide setting in code; BUI_GPU=0 turns the app-wide defaults off, but a window that asks for the GPU itself still gets it. Where no device can start, BUI quietly stays on the CPU (BUI_GPU_DEBUG=1 says why).

Which one? A tool window, form or settings panel: the CPU (lightest on memory, idles at zero). A large or HiDPI window, lots of animation, thousands of items: the GPU (about half the CPU per frame, or less, for about 10 MB more RAM plus GPU memory). Servers and tests: the CPU. macOS: the CPU, for now (a GPU renderer there is coming soon).

More: Rendering.

19. Damage rendering

Leave a BUI window open and walk away: it uses no CPU at all. Hover a button, and BUI redraws that button, not the window.

  1. A change marks only its widget's rectangle as dirty (popups get a margin for their shadow).
  2. Dirty rectangles merge (up to 24 per window).
  3. If nothing is dirty, the loop doesn't render; it sleeps until the next input or timer.
  4. Only the dirty regions are redrawn, clipped to their rectangles.
  5. The raster compares the new pixels with the last frame in 64×32 tiles; a redraw that changed nothing reports nothing.
  6. Only damaged tiles reach the screen (Win32 copies them, X11 sends each rectangle with XPutImage, Cocoa invalidates them, the GPU presents dirty rectangles).

On the full component demo, that's about 0.7 ms for a complete frame and about 0.05 ms for a hover or number-scrub frame. Animations run only while something moves, paced to the display. More: Damage rendering.

20. Window hosts

A window host puts a kit context in a top-level window and feeds it input.

Host Where Notes

X11 (kit_window_x11.c) Linux; Wayland through XWayland Input mapping after Blender's GHOST. Xft.dpi scaling. libX11 is loaded when the first window opens.

21. Text and fonts

Your app's text looks the same on Windows, Linux and macOS, and it looks like Blender's:

  • Inter, Blender's UI font, is embedded (the variable version, with optical-size and weight axes). UI text is 11 pt at scale 1.
  • Rendered like Blender's BLF: BUI vendors FreeType 2.13.3 and renders with light hinting, Blender's gamma-1.43 coverage table, Inter's optical size, a real bold instance, no kerning (as in Blender), and Blender's text shadows. With BUI_TEXT_FREETYPE=OFF, stb_truetype rasterizes instead.
  • On the GPU, glyphs are drawn from their outlines with Slug by default, or from a per-glyph atlas like Blender's (BUI_SLUG=0, bui.set_slug(False), .slug(false), BUI_gpu_set_slug(0)).
  • Other fonts: BUI_FONT=path.ttf replaces Inter, BUI_FONT_DIR adds a folder to search first, blenderui::add_font (Rust) and BUI_text_add_font (C) register faces from memory, and CSS @font-face loads local files.
  • Windows' GDI text is opt-in (-DBUI_TEXT_GDI=ON, Rust feature gdi-text): ClearType-style hinting and system fonts, without Slug.

Limits worth knowing: no per-glyph font fallback yet (missing characters show as boxes), no IME, right-to-left text is reordered but not shaped, no OpenType features. Font fallback and IME are coming soon. More: Text and fonts.

27. C and embedding

The kit's concepts: nodes made by type name (frame, slider, button, panel, tree, canvas, filebrowser ...), properties set by name, Tk's geometry managers (pack, grid, place) in C, a context that owns input, popups, focus and undo, a host that receives events, and windows. A custom node draws and handles input itself; Dear ImGui runs on BUI that way. Guide: docs/c-api.md.

To embed BUI in your own renderer, render the kit into a BuiRaster and blit it (as bui.qt.BuiCanvas does inside Qt). On the same code, blenderui shows its first frame about 5× sooner than gpui and gpui-fast, spends about 8× less CPU getting there, and on the CPU renderer uses half the memory. Idle, gpui keeps about 1.2 % of a core busy; blenderui uses none.

Laptops can't report energy per app, so battery cost is measured by the CPU time an app causes: the CPU it spends starting up, and the CPU it uses over 20 seconds while the window sits idle (what drains a battery while an app is open). BUI redraws only when something changes and otherwise sleeps, so idle use is near zero on either renderer. The GPU renderer starts a little slower and uses more memory (the GPU device), and pays off on large, animated scenes (below). Node's event loop accounts for the JavaScript idle figure, Python's times include starting the interpreter, and memory doesn't count GPU memory.

The GPU renderer is off by default. Turn it on with Application::new().gpu(true), tk.Tk(gpu=True), bui.set_gpu(True) or BUI_GPU=1:

  • Every primitive is one instance of a single shader, so a frame is a few instanced draw calls (Direct3D 11 on Windows, OpenGL 3.3 on Linux).
  • Text and images are cached in atlases.
  • Frames render into a persistent target, so only damaged regions redraw.
  • On Windows, presentation uses a flip-model swap chain with dirty rects.

Its shaders evaluate the software raster's formulas: the parity test finds 10 of 172,800 pixels that differ by more than 3/255, on both backends.

gpui-fast's heavy-scene frame rate varies between sessions on this laptop (30–60 fps), so compare within one session. Method, raw data and how to rerun: bindings/rust/bench/README.md.

33. Run the benchmarks yourself

Every number above comes from a tool in this repo. Build in release mode, close other heavy apps, and plug the laptop in. Run one benchmark (and one build) at a time.

Start time and battery: the five ways and gpui (bench/, Windows). The same settings window written each way, on the CPU and the GPU renderer, plus one gpui-syntax file compiled for blenderui, gpui and gpui-fast. It reports start time, CPU used to start, memory and idle CPU, and writes bench/results.json.

cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build --config Release --target buipy  # Python extension
cd bindings/node && npm run build && cd ../..                                # Node addon
cd bindings/rust && cargo build --release --example bench_app && cd ../..    # Rust app
cd bindings/rust/bench && cargo build --release --bins && cd ../../..        # gpui comparison

Frame cost: 100, 1,000 and 3,000 animated cells, against gpui and gpui-fast (bindings/rust/bench/, Windows). A 1000×800 window filled with N rounded, numbered cells, in three modes:

  • anim: every cell changes every frame, the worst case.
  • one: one cell changes per frame, like a hover or a ticking value.
  • idle: nothing changes.

Each app measures its own CPU cycles, frames and memory, and run.py adds GPU utilisation and GPU memory from Windows' performance counters.

cd bindings/rust/bench
set GPUI_FXC_PATH=C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\bin\10.0.19041.0\x64\fxc.exe   # gpui needs fxc.exe

35. Environment variables

Most are read by the C library, so they work the same from every language. On/off variables look at the first character: 1, y, Y, t or T is on. Where a variable and an app-wide API call set the same thing, the variable wins.

Variable What it does
BUI_GPU 1 draws native windows on the GPU (Direct3D 11 / OpenGL 3.3). Overrides bui.set_gpu(), Application::gpu(), BUI_gpu_set_default(). 0 turns those defaults off; a window that asks for the GPU itself still gets it.
BUI_SLUG GPU text: 1 from glyph outlines (Slug, the default), 0 from a per-glyph atlas.
BUI_GPU_DEBUG 1 prints why the GPU renderer couldn't start.
BUI_GPU_WARP 1 (Windows) creates the Direct3D 11 device on WARP, the software rasterizer. Handy in VMs and CI.
BUI_GPU_MAX_TEXTURE Testing: the largest texture side the GPU renderers give one image (at least 64), so images over it are tiled as on devices with a small limit.
BUI_GPU_EGL default or surfaceless (Linux): the EGL platform for offscreen GPU rendering.
BUI_RASTER_THREADS 1 to 8 (Windows): the most threads the software raster uses for big canvases.
BUI_PROFILE Prints frame times every 60 frames. Any value turns it on, even 0.
BUI_THEME dark (default) or light: Blender's theme, when the app doesn't set one.
BUI_UI_SCALE A fixed UI scale (1.25, 1.5 ...) instead of the display's. Clamped to 0.5–4.

40. Status and roadmap

Known limitations. Read these before you pick BUI for something you will ship. The tables below have the details.

  • No accessibility support. BUI draws its own widgets and does not talk to the platform's accessibility APIs (UI Automation on Windows, AT-SPI on Linux, NSAccessibility on macOS), so screen readers can't see them. Don't use it for software that has to be accessible. Accessibility is planned.
  • Text. Blender's bundled Inter font only (system fonts only with the Windows GDI option). No per-glyph font fallback (missing characters show as boxes), no input methods (IME), right-to-left text is reordered but not shaped, and no OpenType features.
  • It doesn't look native. BUI looks like Blender: its Dark and Light themes (other Blender theme files can't be loaded yet). It doesn't follow your operating system's theme, accent color or fonts.
  • Rendering. The CPU rasterizer is the default and works everywhere. The optional GPU renderer is Direct3D 11 on Windows and OpenGL 3.3 on Linux. There is none on macOS (no Metal): macOS always draws on the CPU. Direct3D 12, Vulkan, Metal and WebGPU backends don't exist yet.
  • Platforms. Windows and Linux (X11; Wayland through XWayland) are the supported ones. macOS is experimental: checked by CI and tried by hand on two Apple Silicon Macs, and JavaScript windows are headless there. The npm packages are prebuilt for Windows x64 only.
  • Retained mode, no visual editor. BUI keeps a tree of nodes, like Blender's own UI; it is not an immediate-mode library. There is no drag-and-drop UI designer: you write the UI in code.
  • Performance numbers come from one machine, a Windows 11 laptop (Ryzen 7 5800U). Linux and macOS haven't been measured yet.
  • The home page demos are browser sketches, not the native engine (the page says so). Run the Python, Rust or JavaScript examples to feel the real widgets. A WebAssembly build is planned.
  • It's a port, not Blender unchanged. Widget drawing and interaction are ported from Blender's UI sources, with edits (each marked BUI:), and the rest of Blender (its data system, window manager and operators) isn't included. There is no automated sync with Blender's releases.
  • Partial areas: Qt syntax (about 24%), CSS (261 of 745 properties render), video has no audio, and image formats such as AVIF, EXR, TIFF, JPEG XL and HEIC aren't supported.
  • License. GPL: a program that includes BUI is distributed under the GPL too (why).

More languages Lua (a community pull request is in review), Ruby, Go (through cgo), C#, Zig, Swift, Kotlin and MyGo over the same C header; Godot, Unity and Bevy; Flutter

Our roadmap has no dates on it. Like a good render, it's done when the noise goes away.

41. FAQ

Do I need Blender installed? No. BUI contains the parts of Blender's UI code it needs and builds on its own.
Is it really my unchanged tkinter app? Yes. blenderui-tk app.py makes import tkinter return BUI's implementation, which covers every public tkinter and ttk name. Nine real programs are tested to behave identically on the standard library and on BUI. See the limitations for the few differences.
Is it a web browser in Rust? No. There's no browser engine and no network. BUI takes HTML elements and CSS as a UI language: they are laid out with taffy and drawn by BUI's engine, with Blender's widgets where you ask for them, in a native window. JavaScript is optional: the Rust crate needs none, and the JavaScript packages drive the same engine.
Is the Dear ImGui support a re-implementation? No. It's the real Dear ImGui (vendored, MIT), running on a BUI backend, so every function behaves as upstream. The optional Blender-widgets build swaps only how ImGui's widgets are drawn and how they react to the mouse, by compiling an edited copy of imgui_widgets.cpp.
How is it different from Electron, Electrobun or GPUIX?
  • Electron ships Chromium with every app: on the order of 100 MB or more.
  • Electrobun runs on Bun and renders in the system's webview. It's small to download, but the UI is still a browser page.
  • GPUIX, like BUI, renders React natively: React drives Zed's GPUI.
BUI also renders natively, with Blender's widgets, a much larger part of CSS, Tailwind, and hooks backed by signals. bui build makes a 5 MB executable that reaches its first frame in about 70 ms.
Do the macros cost performance? rsx!, #[component], css! and tw! expand at compile time into the same builder calls you would write by hand. Tailwind classes are compiled to CSS once, on first use. Hooks are a few nanoseconds per read or write.
Can I change the colors? Yes. Switch between Blender's Dark and Light themes at run time (Themes), color individual widgets in every API, and use full CSS on plain HTML elements in Rust and JavaScript. Loading any other Blender theme file is coming soon.
Does it run on my Mac? Yes, with caveats. The Cocoa host is experimental, but it has been tried by hand on two Apple Silicon Macs (the bugs they found are fixed) and CI builds and tests it on Apple Silicon and Intel runners. Nobody has tried an Intel Mac by hand yet, it draws on the CPU (there is no Metal renderer), and JavaScript windows are headless there. Python can always fall back to the Tk window (BUI_HOST=tk). If you try it, the notes in docs/macos-testing.md say what to report.
Can I use BUI from Vue, Angular, Ruby, Go or Lua? Not yet, but people have asked and they are on the roadmap. Vue and Angular would be thin adapters over @blender-ui/native, the layer React and Svelte already share (how to add a framework). Ruby and Go (through cgo) would call the C kit, BUI_kit.h, which has been versioned since 0.4.1. A Lua binding is in review as a community pull request. If you want one sooner, open an issue or a pull request: CONTRIBUTING.md says how.
Is it ready for production? Much of it is complete and tested (the C kit, tkinter, the components, Rust, Dear ImGui, JavaScript), and some parts are partial or experimental (Qt syntax, parts of CSS and text, macOS). Status and roadmap shows which is which. Pin your version, and test on the platforms you ship.
Who wrote it? LLMs. Not in the way you think. Instead of porting it, we asked an LLM to remove everything that isn't UI logic, and then ported the drawing and interaction code from Blender's sources. Turns out LLMs are better at removing than at generating. We call it Vibe-Pruning.
Why GPL? BUI is derived from Blender's source code, so it follows Blender's licensing: the whole is under the GNU GPL, version 3 or later, and individual files keep their own compatible license (`GPL-2.0-or-later` for the files that come from Blender).
Is it immediate mode? Is there a visual UI editor? BUI is retained-mode: it keeps a tree of nodes, like Blender's own UI, and redraws only what changed. There is no visual UI editor yet; you write the UI in code (tkinter, Qt-style, Blender components, Rust, JavaScript or C).
Is the C API stable? Not before 1.0, but it is versioned: BUI_kit.h has BUI_KIT_VERSION_* macros and BK_version() reports the library's version, the same number as the Python, Rust and npm packages. Every change that breaks existing code is listed under "C API changes" in the changelog. Pin a release number, not a commit. From 1.0 it follows semantic versioning (details).
Is BUI accessible to screen readers? Not yet. See the known limitations.
Can I use BUI in a commercial app? The GPL allows commercial use. What it asks is that when you distribute a program that includes BUI, you distribute it under the GPL too, with its source code available. If that doesn't fit your project, talk to a lawyer before you ship. (This is a summary, not legal advice.)

Star History

42. Contributing and publishing

Contributions are welcome: bug reports, missing tkinter/Qt behavior, CSS features, platform hosts and docs. If you have a Mac, running the Cocoa host and reporting what happens is one of the most useful things you can do right now. Read CONTRIBUTING.md first, and please follow the Code of Conduct. Report security issues privately, as SECURITY.md describes.

Releases go to PyPI (blenderui, wheels built by CI on a v* tag), crates.io (the eight Rust crates, in dependency order) and npm (@blender-ui/native, @blender-ui/react). The steps are in docs/publishing.md.

43. License and credits

License. BUI follows Blender's licensing. BUI as a whole is licensed under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later (the text is in LICENSE). Individual files may have a different, but compatible license: the files that come from Blender keep Blender's SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0-or-later header, and new files carry the same one. Third-party parts keep their own licenses:

Part What it does in BUI License
Blender sources Widget drawing, interaction rules, theme, icons, blenlib, GHOST window code, the File Browser and node editor GPL-2.0-or-later
Dear ImGui by Omar Cornut The immediate-mode GUI that runs on BUI MIT
Inter by Rasmus Andersson The embedded UI font, as in Blender (gpu/extern/Inter-LICENSE.txt) SIL Open Font License 1.1
FreeType 2.13.3 Glyph loading, hinting and rendering, like Blender's BLF FreeType License or GPLv2 (dual-licensed)
stb_truetype by Sean Barrett Font metrics and character maps, and the fallback rasterizer Public domain
NanoSVG by Mikko Mononen, as edited by Blender Rasterizing Blender's SVG icons Zlib
Wuffs by Google Decoding PNG, GIF, BMP, TGA and QOI images MIT or Apache-2.0 (used as MIT)
libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 Decoding JPEG images IJG, BSD-3-Clause and zlib
libwebp 1.6.0 Decoding WebP images, including animation BSD-3-Clause
Slug by Eric Lengyel The GPU glyph coverage algorithm (shader code "Copyright 2017 by Eric Lengyel") MIT
Tailwind CSS The v4 default theme values behind the Tailwind support MIT

The Rust and JavaScript bindings also depend on crates and packages such as taffy, napi-rs, React and QuickJS, each under its own license.

The full license texts of everything above, and of every Rust crate BUI's packages are built from, are in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. It ships inside the Python wheels, the npm packages and the crates, and python tools/gen_notices.py regenerates it.

Acknowledgments. Thank you to:

  • Blender and its community: the UI this project is built from, including its GHOST window code and blenlib.
  • Dear ImGui by Omar Cornut: the immediate-mode GUI that runs on BUI.
  • taffy: flexbox, grid and block layout for the Rust crate.
  • Tailwind CSS: the v4 theme behind the Tailwind support.
  • FreeType: glyph rendering, as in Blender.
  • stb_truetype: font metrics and the fallback rasterizer.
  • NanoSVG by Mikko Mononen: the icon rasterizer, via Blender's edited copy.
  • Inter by Rasmus Andersson: the embedded UI font, as in Blender.
  • Slug by Eric Lengyel: the GPU glyph coverage algorithm.
  • gpui, zopra and Leptos: the APIs the Rust syntax follows.

BUI is Blender's UI, minus the default cube. You're free to add your own.
content_text:
Blender's user interface, as a library you can use from Python, Rust, JavaScript (React, Svelte), C, C++ and Dear ImGui. People spent decades building and optimizing Blender's GUI. It's battery and memory efficient, and super duper fast. We decoupled it, to give everyone a chance to build their own products with it. It supports multiple languages and frameworks, so you won't miss a beat! Website and full documentation: bui.preetham.top · Chat: Discord This README is a small book. Read it front to back for the whole story, or jump to the chapter you need. Every chapter links to a longer guide in docs/ or on the website when there's more to say. Contents Part I: Welcome What BUI is Why BUI exists Who it's for Pick your language Features at a glance A gallery Part II: Getting started Install First app: tkinter First app: Blender components First app: Qt syntax First app: Rust, in rsx and gpui builders First app: JavaScript and React First app: Dear ImGui First app: C Part III: Concepts How it works Blender's widgets and interactions Three looks: HTML, styled and Blender components Rendering on the CPU and the GPU Damage rendering Window hosts Text and fonts Themes: dark and light Part IV: Guides by language Python Rust JavaScript and React Dear ImGui C and embedding Where the docs live Part V: Performance Before you read the numbers Start time and battery Frame times JavaScript and React: startup and animation Run the benchmarks yourself Part VI: Reference Platforms Environment variables Building from source and CMake options Coverage Repository layout Examples Part VII: The project Status and roadmap FAQ Contributing and publishing License and credits Part I: Welcome 1. What BUI is BUI takes the user interface of Blender (its widget drawing, its interaction rules and its look) and turns it into a standalone UI library with a small C core. Your code builds the widget tree and handles callbacks. Layout, input, drawing and presenting all happen in fast native code, on the CPU or the GPU. At the heart of BUI is the kit: a small runtime written in C. The kit holds every widget in one tree, lays them out, handles the mouse and keyboard, and draws them the way Blender does. The drawing code is a C port of Blender's own widget code, and the interaction follows Blender's rules. On top of the kit sit bindings: thin layers that let Python, Rust, JavaScript, C++ and Dear ImGui talk to it. What BUI is not: Not Blender. It contains the parts of Blender's UI code it needs and builds on its own. You don't need Blender installed, and you don't need to know Blender to use it. Not a browser. The Rust and JavaScript sides use HTML and CSS as a UI language, but there's no browser engine, no webview and no network. Not a re-imagining. The widget drawing is ported from Blender's interface_widgets.cc, and the Dear ImGui support runs the real Dear ImGui. 2. Why BUI exists Blender's interface is famous for how it feels. You press a number field and drag: the cursor vanishes, the value glides under your hand, and you never hit the edge of the screen. You type 2*pi into a field and it just works. You type "ad cu" into a menu and it finds "Add Cube". Millions of artists have these habits in their hands. That interface is also fast and frugal. It redraws only what changed, sleeps when nothing does, and starts in milliseconds. BUI exists so that any app, in any language, can have both: Blender's feel, and Blender's efficiency. 3. Who it's for You have a tkinter app and wish it looked less like 1998. Run it on BUI, unchanged. You're building a tool for artists who already know Blender. Give them the panels, sliders and shortcuts their hands expect. You write Rust or React and want a native desktop UI without shipping a browser. You use Dear ImGui and want it to look and feel like Blender, with one build flag. You're curious how a UI toolkit works. The source is readable, and the concepts are explained in plain words. Before you ship something with BUI, read the known limitations: no accessibility support yet, no input methods, and it looks like Blender, not like your operating system. 4. Pick your language You can drive BUI many ways, and all of them share the same C runtime, so they all get the same widgets and interactions: You write You get Status tkinter code, even existing programs, unchanged Blender-styled apps; every tkinter and ttk API Complete Qt-style Python (QWidget, layouts, clicked.connect) The common subset of Qt widgets Partial Blender components (Panel, NumberSlider, PieMenu, the node editor ...) 45 native Blender widgets and editors, from Python; ten of them also from Rust and JavaScript Complete Rust: HTML + CSS + Tailwind, HTML-like markup (rsx! / view!), hooks, or gpui / zopra syntax A web-like framework: HTML that looks like a browser's, Blender's look with styled, and Blender components (, {/* a Blender component */} ) } render(, { title: "Counter", width: 360, height: 200, gpu: true }) bun app.jsx # run it (Bun reads JSX directly) npx bui build app.jsx # or ship it: app.exe, one 7 MB file Without React, @blender-ui/native gives you a DOM-like API: const { App, signal } = require("@blender-ui/native") const app = new App({ gpu: true }) const win = app.window({ title: "Hello", width: 360, height: 200 }) win.body.className = "m-0 p-6 flex flex-col gap-3 bg-[#2b2b2b] text-[#e6e6e6]" const clicks = signal(0) const label = win.createElement("span") label.textContent = clicks // follows the signal const button = win.createElement("button") button.textContent = "Add one" button.addEventListener("click", () => clicks.value++) win.body.appendChild(label) win.body.appendChild(button) These snippets are small. This is a larger example, a task list in React, and not the output of the code above: A task list in React (examples/site/js/todo_react.js); the DOM-like version draws the same Node.js 18+ or Bun. Prebuilt for Windows x64; on Linux, build the addon from source (npm run build in bindings/node) and windows are native. Guide: docs/javascript.md. 13. First app: Dear ImGui The real Dear ImGui 1.93 runs on BUI: BUI's windows, input, CPU/GPU renderer, Blender's theme and the Inter font. Existing ImGui code compiles unchanged. C++: #include "imgui.h" #include "imgui_impl_bui.h" // see examples/imgui_demo.cpp static void frame(void*) { ImGui::ShowDemoWindow(); ImGui::Begin("Hello"); static float v = 0.5f; ImGui::SliderFloat("Value", &v, 0.0f, 1.0f); ImGui::End(); } int main() { ImGui::CreateContext(); ImGui_ImplBUI_App* app = ImGui_ImplBUI_CreateApp("Demo", 1280, 800, frame, nullptr); ImGui_ImplBUI_RunApp(app); ImGui_ImplBUI_DestroyApp(app); ImGui::DestroyContext(); } Python: import blenderui.imgui as imgui # C: cimgui.h · Rust: the blenderui-imgui crate state = {"value": 0.5} def frame(): imgui.show_demo_window() imgui.begin("Hello") _, state["value"] = imgui.slider_float("Value", state["value"], 0.0, 1.0) imgui.end() imgui.run(frame, title="Hello", size=(1280, 800)) C (cimgui.h, cimgui conventions: ImGui_Button, ImGui_ButtonEx, and the backend in cimgui_impl_bui.h) and Rust (blenderui-imgui) work the same way: use blenderui_imgui as imgui; fn main() { let mut value = 0.5f32; imgui::run("Hello", [1280, 800], move || { imgui::show_demo_window(); imgui::begin("Hello"); imgui::slider_float("Value", &mut value, 0.0, 1.0); imgui::end(); }); } Build with -DBUI_IMGUI_BLENDER_WIDGETS=ON (or the Rust feature blender-widgets) and ImGui's widgets become Blender's own: DragFloat is Blender's drag-to-scrub number field (Shift for precision, Ctrl to snap), SliderFloat Blender's number slider, checkboxes drag-toggle, menus and combos get Blender's menus. The rest of the ImGui API is unchanged. (The PyPI wheel is built without it, so from Python you get ImGui's own widgets in Blender's theme unless you build from source.) Dear ImGui's own demo with BUI_IMGUI_BLENDER_WIDGETS=ON: number fields, sliders, color rows and panel headers are Blender's A larger example, a scene inspector, once with ImGui's stock widgets and once with Blender's: The same ImGui code: ImGui's widgets (left) and the Blender-widgets build (right) (examples/site/imgui_inspector.cpp) Guide, coverage and the stock look: docs/imgui.md. 14. First app: C The kit's API is one header, kit/include/BUI_kit.h, and it doubles as the reference: every function has a one-line comment. This is a shortened examples/kit_hello.c: a slider and a button in a native window. #include #include "BUI_kit.h" static void on_event(void *data, BKNode *node, int kind, void *ref, double a, double b) { if (kind == BK_EV_CLICK) printf("clicked %s\n", BK_get_str(node, "text")); else if (kind == BK_EV_CHANGE) printf("%s = %g\n", BK_get_str(node, "label"), BK_get_num(node, "value")); } int main(void) { BKNode *root = BK_node_new("frame"); /* everything is a node */ BK_set_num(root, "padding", 8); /* configured by property name */ BKNode *size = BK_node_new("slider"); BK_set_str(size, "label", "Size"); BK_set_num(size, "max", 10); BK_set_num(size, "value", 2.5); BK_node_add(root, size, -1); BK_geom_set_manager(size, BK_GEOM_PACK); /* Tk's packer, in C */ BK_geom_set(size, "fill", 1); BKNode *apply = BK_node_new("button"); BK_set_str(apply, "text", "Apply"); BK_node_add(root, apply, -1); BK_geom_set_manager(apply, BK_GEOM_PACK); BKContext *ctx = BK_context_new(root); /* input, focus, popups, undo */ BKHost host = {0}; host.emit = on_event; /* the window fills in the rest */ BK_context_set_host(ctx, &host); if (BK_window_supported()) { /* Win32, X11 or Cocoa */ BKWindow *win = BK_window_new(ctx, "BUI from C", 320, 120); BK_window_show(win); BK_window_run(); BK_window_free(win); } BK_context_free(ctx); BK_node_free(root); return 0; } cmake -S . -B build -DBUI_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON cmake --build build --target bui_kit_hello The window below is a bigger program than the one above, a modifier stack: A bigger C program: a modifier stack (examples/site/kit_modifiers.c) Without a window system, render into a raster instead (BK_render(ctx, raster, w, h, full)), which is also how tests and screenshots work. Guide: docs/c-api.md. Part III: Concepts 15. How it works your code: tkinter Qt components Dear ImGui (C++/C/Python/Rust) Rust: rsx! / HTML / CSS / Tailwind / hooks JS / React │ │ │ │ │ │ └──── Python: options, signals │ ImGui core + BUI backend └── style cascade + taffy layout ◄────┘ │ │ │ C kit (kit/): node tree · geometry · input & interaction · Blender widget drawing · undo · animation · themes · Blender search/expr │ renderer: damage-driven software raster (parallel) or GPU (Direct3D 11 / OpenGL 3.3, instanced, opt-in) │ window: native Win32 / X11 / Cocoa window · stdlib Tk window · headless (tests, screenshots) Your code, in any language above, creates widgets and says what happens when they change. The kit keeps them in one tree, lays them out and handles input, following Blender's rules. The renderer draws them, on the CPU by default or on the GPU if you ask. Damage rendering keeps it cheap: a change redraws only the rectangle it touched, and an idle window uses no CPU at all. What's under the hood: Blender's real UI code. Widget drawing is a C port of Blender's interface_widgets.cc (round_box_edges, widgetbase_draw, the shape tables), and interaction follows interface_handlers.cc. Color math, rects, text cursors, string search and expression evaluation are Blender's blenlib, copied in. A few interface files (string search, text-edit undo, float precision) are copied into kit/intern/blender/ and edited for the kit. The X11 and Cocoa hosts follow Blender's GHOST; the Win32 host is BUI's own. One node tree. Every widget is one kit node. The C kit owns layout, hit testing, hover, focus, drags, menus, tooltips, undo and animation. Damage rendering. A change marks only its widget's rectangle, and only changed tiles reach the screen. Thin bindings. Python, Rust and JavaScript keep only what their syntax layer needs. More: ARCHITECTURE.md and How it works. 16. Blender's widgets and interactions These rules live in the C kit, so they work the same everywhere Blender widgets are drawn: the Python components, tkinter and Qt syntax, the Rust and JavaScript Blender components and form controls inside styled, ImGui's Blender-widgets build, and every C kit widget. Drag to scrub. Press a number field and drag sideways. The cursor hides and wraps, so you never hit the screen edge, and comes back where the drag started. A float moves one click step per pixel; Shift moves at a tenth of the speed; Esc cancels and restores the value. Ctrl snaps with Blender's rules: unbounded floats to whole units, angles to 10°, sliders to 0.1, 1 or 10 depending on their range, integers to multiples of 10. Click to type, and type math: Blender's expression evaluator (expr_pylike_eval.cc) turns 2*pi, 90/4, min(4, 3) or x if c else y into numbers. This works in Blender number fields and sliders; plain text fields keep what you type as text. Shortcuts on any value: Backspace resets to the default, - negates, Ctrl+Wheel steps, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy and paste, right-click opens Copy, Paste and Reset. Several fields at once. Drag down over a column of number fields to collect them, then sideways to change them together. Drag across checkboxes (or panel headers) to set them all in one stroke. Panels collapse with Blender's animation; Ctrl+click opens one and closes the others; drag the grip to reorder. Menus work press-drag-release or click; hover switches menu-bar menus; pie menus open around the pointer. Menu search is Blender's string search: start typing in any open menu. It matches word initials ("ad cu" finds "Add Cube"), forgives typos, and ranks your recent picks first. Undo everywhere. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z work on every UI edit, and inside a text field while you type. A burst of typing or a multi-field drag is one step. Float precision follows Blender: small values show the decimals they need. Tooltips appear after Blender's half-second delay. Coming soon: typing values with units ("2 m"), Blender's search-as-you-type popups, and widget drag and drop. More: Blender's widgets. 17. Three looks: HTML, styled and Blender components In Rust and JavaScript you pick the look per element: You write You get Plain HTML: // Blender's look inside } div().child(Checkbox().checked(true)).child(Button().child("Apply")) // gpui syntax import { render, NumberSlider, Button } from "@blender-ui/react" // , // DOM API: win.createElement("NumberSlider") cargo run --example forms: plain HTML, inside styled, and the Blender components The same markup, plain (left) and inside styled (right). Plain HTML looks the same in both themes. Blender components from Rust (site_components.rs) Python's Blender components (Panel, PieMenu, the node editor ...) are a separate, larger set. 18. Rendering on the CPU and the GPU BUI has two renderers, and they draw the same pixels. The software raster (gpu/intern/gpu_raster.c) is the default. It draws anti-aliased shapes with signed-distance coverage, like Blender's widget shaders, into one frame buffer, compares it with the last frame in 64×32 tiles, and reports only the tiles that changed. Big canvases draw in parallel bands on Windows (BUI_RASTER_THREADS). It needs nothing from your graphics card and uses the least memory. The GPU renderer is opt-in: Direct3D 11 on Windows (gpu/intern/gpu_d3d11.c) and OpenGL 3.3 core on Linux (gpu/intern/gpu_gl.c). It's modeled on Blender's instanced widget drawing: each primitive is one 128-byte instance of a single uber-shader, so a frame is a few instanced draw calls. Text and images are cached in atlases. Frames render into a persistent target, so only damaged regions redraw; on Windows, a flip-model swap chain presents dirty rectangles. On Linux, libGL, libEGL and libX11 are loaded at run time (GLX for windows, EGL for offscreen), so no GL headers are needed, and BUI falls back to the CPU where OpenGL is missing. The shaders evaluate the software raster's formulas: the parity test finds 10 of 172,800 pixels that differ by more than 3/255, on both backends. Turn the GPU on: Where How Python bui.set_gpu(True) before creating windows; tkinter syntax also tk.Tk(gpu=True) Rust Application::new().gpu(true), or WindowOptions { gpu: Some(true), .. } JavaScript new App({ gpu: true }), or React's render(..., { gpu: true }) C BUI_gpu_set_default(1), or BK_window_set_gpu(win, 1) Any app, no code change BUI_GPU=1 BUI_GPU=1 overrides the app-wide setting in code; BUI_GPU=0 turns the app-wide defaults off, but a window that asks for the GPU itself still gets it. Where no device can start, BUI quietly stays on the CPU (BUI_GPU_DEBUG=1 says why). Which one? A tool window, form or settings panel: the CPU (lightest on memory, idles at zero). A large or HiDPI window, lots of animation, thousands of items: the GPU (about half the CPU per frame, or less, for about 10 MB more RAM plus GPU memory). Servers and tests: the CPU. macOS: the CPU, for now (a GPU renderer there is coming soon). More: Rendering. 19. Damage rendering Leave a BUI window open and walk away: it uses no CPU at all. Hover a button, and BUI redraws that button, not the window. A change marks only its widget's rectangle as dirty (popups get a margin for their shadow). Dirty rectangles merge (up to 24 per window). If nothing is dirty, the loop doesn't render; it sleeps until the next input or timer. Only the dirty regions are redrawn, clipped to their rectangles. The raster compares the new pixels with the last frame in 64×32 tiles; a redraw that changed nothing reports nothing. Only damaged tiles reach the screen (Win32 copies them, X11 sends each rectangle with XPutImage, Cocoa invalidates them, the GPU presents dirty rectangles). On the full component demo, that's about 0.7 ms for a complete frame and about 0.05 ms for a hover or number-scrub frame. Animations run only while something moves, paced to the display. More: Damage rendering. 20. Window hosts A window host puts a kit context in a top-level window and feeds it input. Host Where Notes Win32 (kit_window_win32.c) Windows BUI's own host. Per-monitor DPI, vsync-paced animation, clipboard, cursors, window-manager features. X11 (kit_window_x11.c) Linux; Wayland through XWayland Input mapping after Blender's GHOST. Xft.dpi scaling. libX11 is loaded when the first window opens. Cocoa (kit_window_cocoa.m) macOS Experimental. Ported from Blender's GHOST Cocoa code, with Retina scaling. It's checked by CI and has been tried by hand on two Apple Silicon Macs so far; testing notes in docs/macos-testing.md. Tk Python, anywhere A stdlib tkinter window that shows the kit's frame buffer. BUI_HOST=tk forces it; it's also the fallback where no native host works. Headless Everywhere No window: render into a raster for tests and screenshots, with a virtual clock that steps animations exactly. BUI_UI_SCALE=1.5 fixes the UI scale instead of following the display (1 is Blender's default, 20 px widgets). More: Window hosts. 21. Text and fonts Your app's text looks the same on Windows, Linux and macOS, and it looks like Blender's: Inter, Blender's UI font, is embedded (the variable version, with optical-size and weight axes). UI text is 11 pt at scale 1. Rendered like Blender's BLF: BUI vendors FreeType 2.13.3 and renders with light hinting, Blender's gamma-1.43 coverage table, Inter's optical size, a real bold instance, no kerning (as in Blender), and Blender's text shadows. With BUI_TEXT_FREETYPE=OFF, stb_truetype rasterizes instead. On the GPU, glyphs are drawn from their outlines with Slug by default, or from a per-glyph atlas like Blender's (BUI_SLUG=0, bui.set_slug(False), .slug(false), BUI_gpu_set_slug(0)). Other fonts: BUI_FONT=path.ttf replaces Inter, BUI_FONT_DIR adds a folder to search first, blenderui::add_font (Rust) and BUI_text_add_font (C) register faces from memory, and CSS @font-face loads local files. Windows' GDI text is opt-in (-DBUI_TEXT_GDI=ON, Rust feature gdi-text): ClearType-style hinting and system fonts, without Slug. Limits worth knowing: no per-glyph font fallback yet (missing characters show as boxes), no IME, right-to-left text is reordered but not shaped, no OpenType features. Font fallback and IME are coming soon. More: Text and fonts. 22. Themes: dark and light BUI looks like Blender because it uses Blender's theme. It ships two: Blender's Dark theme (the default) and its Light preset. Both are generated by tools/gen_theme.py from Blender's own Blender_Dark.xml and Blender_Light.xml presets, over Blender 5.x's built-in defaults. Switch at run time, and every open window relayouts and redraws: Where Light theme C BK_set_theme("light"); BK_theme_name(), BK_theme_color("region_bg", rgba) Python blenderui.set_theme("light") (also switches the Dear ImGui extension); theme_name(), theme_color(key) Rust blenderui::set_theme("light"), or Application::new().theme("light"); theme_name(), theme_color(key) JavaScript new App({ theme: "light" }), app.setTheme("light"), or React's render(..., { theme: "light" }) Dear ImGui Its Blender style follows the kit's theme (pick it before the backend starts) Any app, no code change BUI_THEME=light (or dark) Widgets, panels, the region background, the styled HTML sheet and ImGui's Blender style all follow the theme. Plain HTML keeps a browser's look either way. Inside each theme you can still color things yourself: bg / fg in tkinter, setStyleSheet in Qt syntax, color= on components, full CSS on HTML in Rust and JavaScript, ImGui's own style colors. BUI also includes Blender's icons: all 781 of Blender's SVG icons, rasterized with Blender's NanoSVG code so they're sharp at any scale. Use them by Blender's name: Button("Add", icon="ADD"), EnumRow(..., icons=[...]). Coming soon: loading any Blender theme file, beyond Dark and Light. More: Theming. Part IV: Guides by language 23. Python pip install blenderui gives you four APIs in one package: tkinter syntax (blenderui.tksyntax): every public tkinter and ttk name (7,846 of 7,846). Run existing programs with blenderui-tk app.py, or call blenderui.tksyntax.install() first. messagebox and simpledialog are Blender-styled, colorchooser is Blender's color picker, and filedialog is Blender's File Browser (BUI_FILEDIALOG=native for the OS dialogs). Look-only Tk options (relief, ttk.Style ...) are accepted, but the look comes from Blender's theme. Guide: docs/tkinter.md. Qt syntax (blenderui.qtsyntax): widgets, layouts (box, grid, form, stacked), signals, QPainter, menus, timers and animations, QFileDialog as Blender's File Browser. Partial: model/view classes, docks, toolbars, splitters and Qt stylesheets are missing. Guide: docs/qt.md. Blender components (blenderui.components): 45 components, from NumberSlider to NodeEditor. Reference: docs/components.md. Dear ImGui (blenderui.imgui), pyimgui-style. Guide: docs/imgui.md. You can mix them in one process: windows, timers and the event loop are shared (bui.host). Every interaction runs in C, so tests can drive widgets headless. On the website: tkinter, Qt syntax, components, headless testing. 24. Rust The blenderui crate is a web-like framework drawn by BUI: every HTML element, CSS, Tailwind, HTML-like markup (rsx! / view!) or gpui-style builders, components and hooks. CSS: selectors level 4, nesting, @layer / @media / @supports / @scope / @container / @font-face / @property, var() and env(), every math function, CSS Color 4 and 5. Part I: Welcome
What BUI is

blocks.html_en: BUI takes the user interface of Blender (its widget drawing, its interaction rules and its look) and turns it into a standalone UI library with a small C core. Your code builds the widget tree and handles callbacks. Layout, input, drawing and presenting all happen in fast native code, on the CPU or the GPU.

sentences.en: BUI takes the user interface of Blender (its widget drawing, its interaction rules and its look) and turns it into a standalone UI library with a small C core.
Your code builds the widget tree and handles callbacks.
Layout, input, drawing and presenting all happen in fast native code, on the CPU or the GPU.

blocks.html_en: At the heart of BUI is the kit: a small runtime written in C. The kit holds every widget in one tree, lays them out, handles the mouse and keyboard, and draws them the way Blender does. The drawing code is a C port of Blender's own widget code, and the interaction follows Blender's rules. On top of the kit sit bindings: thin layers that let Python, Rust, JavaScript, C++ and Dear ImGui talk to it.

sentences.en: At the heart of BUI is the kit: a small runtime written in C.
The kit holds every widget in one tree, lays them out, handles the mouse and keyboard, and draws them the way Blender does.
The drawing code is a C port of Blender's own widget code, and the interaction follows Blender's rules.
On top of the kit sit bindings: thin layers that let Python, Rust, JavaScript, C++ and Dear ImGui talk to it.
What BUI is not:

blocks.html_en: • Not Blender. It contains the parts of Blender's UI code it needs and builds on its own. You don't need Blender installed, and you don't need to know Blender to use it.

sentences.en: Not Blender.

You don't need Blender installed, and you don't need to know Blender to use it.

blocks.html_en: • Not a browser. The Rust and JavaScript sides use HTML and CSS as a UI language, but there's no browser engine, no webview and no network.

sentences.en: Not a browser.
The Rust and JavaScript sides use HTML and CSS as a UI language, but there's no browser engine, no webview and no network.

blocks.html_en: • Not a re-imagining. The widget drawing is ported from Blender's interface_widgets.cc, and the Dear ImGui support runs the real Dear ImGui.

sentences.en: Not a re-imagining.
The widget drawing is ported from Blender's interface_widgets.cc, and the Dear ImGui support runs the real Dear ImGui.
Why BUI exists

blocks.html_en: Blender's interface is famous for how it feels. You press a number field and drag: the cursor vanishes, the value glides under your hand, and you never hit the edge of the screen. You type 2*pi into a field and it just works. You type "ad cu" into a menu and it finds "Add Cube". Millions of artists have these habits in their hands.

sentences.en: Blender's interface is famous for how it feels.
You press a number field and drag: the cursor vanishes, the value glides under your hand, and you never hit the edge of the screen.
You type 2*pi into a field and it just works.
You type "ad cu" into a menu and it finds "Add Cube".
Millions of artists have these habits in their hands.

blocks.html_en: That interface is also fast and frugal. It redraws only what changed, sleeps when nothing does, and starts in milliseconds. BUI exists so that any app, in any language, can have both: Blender's feel, and Blender's efficiency.

sentences.en: That interface is also fast and frugal.

BUI exists so that any app, in any language, can have both: Blender's feel, and Blender's efficiency.

blocks.html_en: • Blender's real UI code. Widget drawing is a C port of Blender's interface_widgets.cc (round_box_edges, widgetbase_draw, the shape tables), and interaction follows interface_handlers.cc. Color math, rects, text cursors, string search and expression evaluation are Blender's blenlib, copied in. A few interface files (string search, text-edit undo, float precision) are copied into kit/intern/blender/ and edited for the kit. The X11 and Cocoa hosts follow Blender's GHOST; the Win32 host is BUI's own.
